content: Gastrointestinal bleeding in children refers to the loss of blood from any part of the digestive tract. In pediatric clinical practice, it is a common reason for children to visit the emergency department. This symptom can be associated with various underlying conditions, including ulcers, gastric or esophageal varices, gastritis, Mallory-Weiss tears, anorectal fissures, allergic colitis, infectious colitis, intussusception, Henoch-Schönlein purpura, and Meckel's diverticulum. Additionally, gastrointestinal bleeding is frequently observed in critically ill children admitted to intensive care units, where it is often caused by stress-induced gastropathy. Regardless of the underlying cause, fasting is commonly recommended in cases of gastrointestinal bleeding due to concerns that eating might interfere with the process of haemostasis or exacerbate the bleeding. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effects and safety of fasting as a measure to promote haemostasis in children with gastrointestinal bleeding. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), Ovid MEDLINE, EMBASE, the Chinese Biomedical Database (CBM), China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI), VIP Database, and Wanfang Data. The search spanned publications from their inception up to May 2016, with no restrictions on language or study setting. However, searches in CNKI and Wanfang Data were limited to the medical field. The inclusion criteria for this review were randomized controlled trials (RCTs) or quasi-RCTs involving children with gastrointestinal bleeding that compared the effects of fasting with feeding. Two independent reviewers screened the search results, and there were no disagreements between them. Despite the extensive search, no RCTs or quasi-RCTs were identified that met the inclusion criteria. Consequently, no studies were available to provide evidence on the effects or safety of fasting compared to feeding for haemostasis in children with gastrointestinal bleeding. In conclusion, there is currently no evidence from RCTs or quasi-RCTs to either support or refute the practice of fasting as a strategy for haemostasis in pediatric patients with gastrointestinal bleeding.
